title: Short Stuff: Tarring and Feathering
summary: Short Stuff episode on tarring and feathering, a punishment used in colonial and revolutionary America, initially on criminals and later by the Sons of Liberty against Loyalists and British sympathizers. The hosts cover the process (stripping, hot pine tar, chicken feathers), the pain and humiliation, the social-class carve-out for wealthy or officer Loyalists, and three cases: William Smith in Norfolk, Virginia in 1766, John Malcolm in Boston in January 1774, and a 1981 Alabama case involving Marietta Macklway and Elizabeth Jamison. The episode opens with banter about whether they had covered the topic before and closes with a sign-off.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Hosts joke about demonstrating the topic and debate whether they have covered tarring and feathering before, mentioning Ridiculous History and a 2011 live show.

segments.title: Origins and purpose of tarring and feathering
segments.summary: Tarring and feathering began as a punishment for criminals in colonial America and was taken up by the Sons of Liberty against those seen as loyal to England. It was used to intimidate, and its peak was the late 1760s and early 1770s, after measures such as the Townshend Acts.

segments.title: Golden age banter
segments.summary: Brief joking exchange about who coined the term Golden Age.

segments.title: How the punishment was carried out
segments.summary: Victims were stripped and covered in hot pine tar, sometimes poured on, which caused blistering; no one is known to have died from it. Chicken feathers were then dumped on them, and they were paraded through town on a cart or rail while being mocked, often with whippings and beatings.

segments.title: Transition to John Malcolm case
segments.summary: The hosts introduce the well-known case of customs official John Malcolm and take a break.

segments.title: John Malcolm tarring and feathering in Boston, 1774
segments.summary: In January 1774, a mob in Boston tarred and feathered customs official John Malcolm after he struck a Patriot supporter, a boy, in the street. A period article described the beating and tarring, and the hosts note the burns. Malcolm had been tarred and feathered before.

segments.title: William Smith case in Norfolk, 1766
segments.summary: Sea captain William Smith was tarred and feathered in Norfolk, Virginia in 1766 by seven men including the mayor, after being accused of tipping off a royal official about smuggling. He was paraded through town, thrown off a wharf, and nearly drowned. The Sons of Liberty and Bostonians began adopting the practice three years later.

segments.title: Who was targeted and social class
segments.summary: Targets were customs officials and people not loyal to the revolution, but wealthy or officer Loyalists were usually spared. Tarring and feathering was an insult that emphasized inferior social status, compared to how a gentleman would be challenged to a duel.

segments.title: 1981 Alabama tarring and feathering
segments.summary: In 1981 in Alabama, Marietta Macklway and her sister held Elizabeth Jamison at shotgun point, cut her hair, and tarred and feathered her because Jamison was set to marry Macklway's ex-husband. Both sisters were arrested, and Jamison washed off the tar and married later that week.

segments.title: Date check and closing banter
segments.summary: The hosts confirm the year was 1981 and joke about the 1980s.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts agree the topic is covered and close the Short Stuff episode, followed by the production credit.
